newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major puts economy at top of poll bid.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major puts economy at top of poll bid.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, trailing badly in polls, pledged on Sunday to fight -- and win -- the looming election on the basis of a booming economy.
Setting the tone for the forthcoming election campaign, Major said Britain faced a watershed year in 1997.
"They can choose a future where prices and mortgage rates are firmly under control," Major said in a New Year message to the chairmen of local Conservative party associations.
"They can choose a future that looks rosy, with the best economic conditions this country has seen for a century...and they can choose a future where British interests will be fought for in Europe.

"Or they can risk a future with an untried, unrealistic alternative. We will win that election, because on all three counts it is too risky to trust Labour with Britain's future," he said in the letter, released by the ruling party on Sunday.
Major also made five pledges to voters.

He promised to cut the basic rate of tax from 23 percent to 20, to keep inflation firmly under control, to ensure house loans remain affordable, to create new jobs and to fight against moves towards a more federal Europe.
But the opposition Labour party, which has a poll lead of 20 points or more with an election due by May at the latest, immediately dismissed Major's rallying cry to key party workers.
"It is a desperate last-ditch effort to win back support before the election," said Labour's deputy leader John Prescott.

"It will fail like every attempt before because the British people want fresh, strong leadership for the future, not the same old personal abuse from the Tories and the same old lies about their record," said Prescott.
Labour leader Tony Blair unveiled five pledges three months ago at his party's last annual conference before the election.

Blair promised to cut primary school class sizes, to get 250,000 unemployed youths into work, to cut hospital waiting lists, to take a tough line on persistent young offenders and to keep both government spending and inflation down.
The Labour leader is expected to call for an early election in his New Year message, due to be unveiled on Monday.

His party has already announced a policy of parliamentary non-cooperation with the government, which earlier this month lost its overall majority in the House of Commons, although it still has 51 more members of parliament than Labour alone.

But Major, who is reported to be planning a lengthy election campaign to wear down Labour's poll lead and to increase his chances of tripping Blair up, said only another Conservative government would safeguard Britain's stability and prosperity.
Major, whose Conservatives have been in office since 1979 without a break, said Labour was making unachievable promises.
"They have made 30 billion pounds ($50.48 billion) worth of spending pledges...The real danger lies in the fact that Labour won't say where the money is coming from," Major said
Major, whose ruling party is deeply divided over plans for European integration, also portayed Blair as soft on Europe.
"He says he would never be isolated in Europe, so he would just follow the crowd...He would undermine our veto -- our right to say 'no' -- in many crucial areas," Major said.

But Major faces a hard fight once parliament returns from its holiday break in two weeks to rein in so-called Conservative Eurosceptics opposed to European integration, whose power over the leadership has grown as the party's majority has dwindled.
